facts.fact: The Earth is divided into three parts: crust, mantle and core.
The core is rich in nickel and iron, hence called the NIFE layer.
The Mohorovicic (Moho) discontinuity separates the crust from the mantle.
The Conrad discontinuity separates the upper crust (SiAl) from the lower crust (SiMa).
The Gutenberg discontinuity separates the mantle from the outer core.
The Lehmann discontinuity separates the outer core from the inner core.
The Repetti discontinuity separates the upper and lower mantle.
SIAL (silica + aluminium) is granitic continental crust; SIMA (silica + magnesium) is basaltic oceanic crust.
Oceanic crust is basaltic and denser than the granitic continental crust.
Oceanic crust is younger than continental crust.
Oxygen is the most abundant element in the Earth's crust.
Aluminium is the most abundant metal in the crust; iron is the most abundant metal in the whole Earth.
The mantle extends from the Moho to a depth of about 2,900 km.
The asthenosphere (upper mantle) is the source of magma.
The outer core is molten (liquid) while the inner core is solid.
The discontinuities top-down are Conrad, Moho, Repetti, Gutenberg, Lehmann ('Commander Mohit is ReGuLar').
P-waves are longitudinal and travel through solids, liquids and gases.
S-waves cannot pass through liquids, which shows that the outer core is molten.
Alfred Wegener proposed the Continental Drift Theory.
Wegener's single supercontinent was Pangaea, surrounded by the ocean Panthalassa.
The Tethys Sea divided Pangaea into Laurasia (north) and Gondwanaland (south).
Harry Hess proposed sea-floor spreading.
Arthur Holmes (1930s) proposed convection currents in the mantle driven by radioactive heat.
Symmetrical paleomagnetic stripes on either side of mid-ocean ridges are the key evidence of sea-floor spreading.
The Nazca plate is a minor plate, not one of the seven major plates.
Divergent (constructive) boundaries form mid-ocean ridges; continental divergence forms rift valleys like the East African Rift.
Convergent (destructive) boundaries form fold mountains (Himalayas) and ocean trenches at subduction zones.
At transform boundaries plates slide past each other; the San Andreas Fault is the best example.
India collided with Asia about 40–50 million years ago, uplifting the Himalayas, which are still rising.
The outpouring of lava during the Indian Plate's movement formed the Deccan Traps.
The focus (hypocentre) is where energy is released inside the Earth; the epicentre is the surface point directly above.
A foreshock precedes the main shock; aftershocks follow it.
Surface (L) waves are the slowest and most destructive earthquake waves.
On the Richter scale each step is about 32 times more energy; two steps about 1,000 times.
The Mercalli scale measures intensity (observed effects), not energy.
The Circum-Pacific Belt ('Pacific Ring of Fire') accounts for about 68% of all earthquakes.
The Alpine–Himalayan belt releases about 15% of the world's earthquake energy.
Nearly 59% of India's land area is prone to moderate or severe earthquakes (NDMA map).
Zone V is India's highest seismic-risk zone — NE India, the Himalayas, Kutch and Andaman–Nicobar.
Shallow quakes are 0–70 km deep, intermediate 70–300 km, deep 300–700 km.
Shield volcanoes are broad and gentle, built of fluid low-viscosity basalt (Mauna Loa).
Intrusive landforms: batholith (largest), dyke (vertical), sill (horizontal), laccolith (dome).
Limestone metamorphoses into marble.
Sandstone metamorphoses into quartzite.
Granite metamorphoses into gneiss.
Coal metamorphoses into anthracite and graphite.
Rocks are igneous (primary), sedimentary (layered, fossils) and metamorphic (from heat and pressure).
Basalt is an igneous rock, not metamorphic.
Feldspar and quartz are the most common minerals in rocks.
The mass extinction of the dinosaurs marks the end of the Cretaceous period.
The geological time scale hierarchy is Eon > Era > Period > Epoch.
Endogenic forces originate within the Earth, powered by internal heat, and build up the surface.
Orogeny is mountain building through folding and faulting.
Exogenic processes such as weathering and erosion are powered by solar energy.
Epeirogeny is broad, continent-wide uplift or warping of the crust.
Weathering is the in-situ breakdown of rock; erosion removes and transports it.
Chemical weathering alters minerals by carbonation, hydration, hydrolysis and oxidation.
Mountain types: fold (Himalayas, Alps), block (Black Forest, Vosges), volcanic (Kilimanjaro, Fujiyama), residual (Aravalli).
A cut-off river meander that survives as a separate water body is an oxbow lake.
A cirque is an armchair-shaped glacial hollow that may hold a tarn lake.
An arete is a steep, sharp ridge between two glacial valleys.
An esker is a winding ridge of glacial debris on a till plain.
A fjord is a steep-sided narrow glacial valley drowned at the coast (Norway).
Barchan dunes are crescent-shaped with tips pointing downwind.
Stalactites and stalagmites are karst (limestone-dissolution) features.
A sea stack is left by the collapse of a sea arch (marine erosion).
A sinkhole is a funnel-shaped karst depression.
A tombolo is a bar connecting an island to the mainland or another island.
A yardang is a streamlined rock ridge carved by wind parallel to the prevailing wind.
Loess is fertile wind-deposited fine silt (e.g. Hwang-Ho basin).
A playa is a temporary shallow salt lake in a desert basin (bolson).
Barren Island in the Andaman Sea is India's only active volcano.
Barren Island has erupted repeatedly after 1991 (e.g. 2017), so it is not dormant.
Narcondam is India's other volcanic island and is regarded as dormant.
About 98% of India's coal comes from the Gondwana rock system.
Kodarma in Jharkhand is famous for mica.
The Dharwar system is rich in metallic minerals (iron, manganese, gold) but not petroleum.
Petroleum in India comes from Tertiary rocks.
The Cuddapah system (Proterozoic) carries iron, manganese, limestone, asbestos and barytes.
Shale gas occurs in the Cambay, Cauvery and Krishna-Godavari basins (UPSC 2015).
Oceanic crust has a density of about 3.0 g/cm³ and continental crust about 2.7 g/cm³.
Oceanic crust is about 5 km thick on average and continental crust about 30 km.
The asthenosphere ('astheno' = weak) extends to about 400 km.
The lithosphere (crust + uppermost mantle) is 10–200 km thick.
The lower mantle, below the asthenosphere, is in a solid state.
Mantle density increases with depth from about 3.3 to 5.7 g/cm³; it is made of iron- and magnesium-rich silicates.
The outer core is about 2,200 km thick at about 4,000–6,000°C.
The inner core is about 1,220 km (radius), solid, at about 5,400°C with density 12.6–13.0 g/cm³.
The P-wave shadow zone lies between about 103° and 142° from the epicentre.
S-waves are not recorded beyond about 103° from the epicentre, so the S-wave shadow zone is larger.
The deepest drilling, the Kola Superdeep Borehole (Russia), reached only about 12 km.
Indirect sources of knowledge of the interior include temperature and pressure gradients, meteorites, gravity, magnetism and seismic waves.
The Earth's mean radius is about 6,371 km.
Wegener proposed continental drift in 1912; the source text dates it to 1922 (his book's later edition).
According to Wegener, drift began about 200 million years ago.
Wegener's forces were the pole-fleeing force (from rotation) and the tidal force; both were too weak to move continents.
Brazil fits into the Gulf of Guinea of Africa (jig-saw fit).
The Caledonian and Hercynian mountains of Europe continue in the Appalachians of the USA.
Glossopteris flora found in India, Australia, South Africa, Falklands and Antarctica shows they were once Gondwana.
Lemurs in India, Madagascar and Africa led to the idea of a linking land called Lemuria.
Mesosaurus skeletons are found only in South Africa and Brazil, now 4,800 km apart.
Tillite (glacial sedimentary rock) of the Gondwana system occurs across India, Africa, Antarctica and Australia.
Placer gold deposits of West Africa were derived from the Brazil plateau.
Rock belts about 2,000 million years old on coastal Brazil match those of western Africa.
Wegener could not explain why drift began only in the Mesozoic era.
Plate tectonics was suggested by McKenzie and Parker (1967) and outlined by Morgan (1968).
Lithospheric plates float on the asthenosphere and are moved by mantle convection currents.
Minor plates include Cocos, Nazca, Arabian, Philippine, Caroline, Fuji, Caribbean, Juan de Fuca, Turkish, Aegean and Iranian.
The Cocos plate lies between Central America and the Pacific plate; the Nazca plate between South America and the Pacific plate.
Older rocks form the continents while younger rocks lie on the ocean floor — evidence of plate tectonics.
India was separated from Asia by the Tethys Sea until about 225 million years ago.
About 140 million years ago the Indian subcontinent lay far south, in the Southern Hemisphere.
The Deccan Trap lava outpouring began about 60 million years ago.
Both continental drift and glacial cycles influenced the evolution of organisms (UPSC 2014).
The 1967 Koynanagar earthquake (6.3) near the Koyna Dam, Maharashtra, is an example of reservoir-induced seismicity.
Human-induced earthquakes are caused by mining, petroleum extraction, artificial lakes and nuclear tests.
Earthquakes of volcanic origin are generally less severe and more limited than tectonic ones.
A series of many small earthquakes for months without a major quake is an earthquake swarm.
Shallow quakes release about 70–85% of earthquake energy, intermediate 12–15%, deep 3–5%.
The shallow 2016 Italy quake (6.2, ~10 km) killed about 300 while a deeper (84 km) Myanmar quake (6.8) killed few — depth matters.
P-waves (compressional/pressure waves) travel at about 5–8 km/s.
S-waves are also called transverse, shear or distortional waves.
Charles F. Richter developed the Richter scale in the 1930s; the moment magnitude scale is better for large quakes.
The Mercalli intensity scale has 12 levels (I–XII).
The largest recorded earthquake was the 1960 Valdivia (Chile) quake of magnitude 9.4–9.6.
The 2004 Indian Ocean earthquake measured 9.1–9.3.
The 1950 Assam–Tibet earthquake measured 8.6.
The 2001 Gujarat earthquake measured 7.7; the 1819 Rann of Kutch quake was 7.7–8.2.
The 2011 Tohoku (Japan) quake measured 9.1 and the 1964 Alaska quake 9.2.
Magnitude classes: 7.0–7.9 major (10–20 a year), 8.0–8.9 great (about one a year).
The Alpine belt runs from Mexico across the Atlantic and Mediterranean through the Alpine–Caucasus ranges to the Himalayas.
Most of Andhra Pradesh lies in seismic Zones II and III.
Volcanoes are classed by activity as active, dormant or extinct.
Shield volcanoes are the largest volcanoes, with short intervals between eruptions (Mauna Kea, Surtsey).
Composite (strato) volcanoes have viscous lava and layers of tephra; examples St. Helens, Vesuvius, Etna, Fuji.
Calderas, the most explosive volcanoes, include Yellowstone and Crater Lake (Oregon).
Flood basalt lava is rich in iron and magnesium and low in silica; it typifies mid-ocean ridge volcanism.
Lava domes form from highly viscous lava piling up near the vent.
A volcanic neck is the solidified conduit exposed when the cone erodes.
Black cotton soil was formed by the weathering of fissure volcanic rock (UPSC 2021).
Ojos del Salado (6,893 m, Chile–Argentina) is the world's highest volcano.
A crater is a summit bowl; a caldera is a much larger collapse depression.
The scientific study of rocks is called petrology.
Feldspar makes up about half of the Earth's crust.
Quartz (silicon + oxygen, hexagonal crystals) is used in radio and radar.
Bauxite, a hydrous oxide of aluminium, is the ore of aluminium.
Mercury is derived from cinnabar.
Dolomite is a double carbonate of calcium and magnesium.
Gypsum is hydrous calcium sulphate, used in cement and fertiliser.
Haematite is the red ore and magnetite the black ore of iron.
Amphibole forms about 7% of the crust (asbestos); mica about 4% (electrical instruments).
Olivine (magnesium, iron, silica) is a greenish crystal; pyroxene is green or black.
Igneous rocks are un-fossiliferous because they form at high temperatures.
Plutonic igneous rocks cool slowly at depth and are coarse-grained (granite).
Extrusive (volcanic) igneous rocks cool quickly and are fine-grained (basalt).
Dyke (intermediate) rocks lie between plutonic and surface rocks and are semi-crystalline.
Igneous rocks are acidic or basic depending on silica content.
Amygdales are gas bubbles in basalt filled with minerals.
Sedimentary rocks form by lithification — compaction and consolidation of sediments.
Sedimentary rocks are stratified and fossiliferous.
Sedimentary rocks are mechanically (sandstone), organically (coal, chalk) or chemically (halite, potash) formed.
Mechanically formed sedimentary rocks like sandstone are the best reservoirs for groundwater and petroleum.
Petroleum comes from the decay of tiny marine organisms in sedimentary rocks.
The arrangement of minerals in layers in metamorphic rocks is called foliation.
Causes of metamorphism are orogenic movements, lava inflow and geodynamic forces.
Clay/shale becomes slate (then phyllite) under heat and schist under pressure.
In the rock cycle, subduction carries crustal rocks into the mantle where they melt into magma.
Ice-deposited sedimentary rocks are till/tillite; wind-deposited sediments are loess.
The Holocene (last 10,000 years) is the epoch of modern man.
The Pleistocene (10,000 years to 2 million years ago) saw the rise of Homo sapiens.
Anthropoid apes evolved in the Oligocene.
Flowering plants and trees expanded in the Miocene.
Rabbits and hares evolved in the Eocene; small mammals (rats, mice) in the Palaeocene.
The Jurassic was the age of dinosaurs (early birds evolved).
Frogs and turtles evolved in the Triassic.
In the Permian reptiles replaced amphibians; it ended in a mass extinction.
The Carboniferous saw the first reptiles and vast coal beds.
Amphibians evolved in the Devonian.
The first plants on land appeared in the Silurian.
The first fish appeared in the Ordovician.
In the Cambrian marine invertebrates dominated and there was no terrestrial life.
Blue-green algae and unicellular bacteria characterise the Archean.
In the Hadean oceans and continents formed with a CO2-rich atmosphere.
The three later eras are Palaeozoic, Mesozoic and Cainozoic.
The Quaternary period comprises the Pleistocene and Holocene epochs.
On the modern chart the dinosaurs' extinction is dated about 66 million years ago (source: 65).
The time scale is used for dating rocks and fossils, correlating strata and resource exploration.
A limitation of the time scale is the incomplete fossil record.
William Morris Davis (1850–1934) founded the science of geomorphology.
Radioactive decay provides about 50% of the Earth's internal heat.
Epeirogenic movements act radially; orogenic movements act tangentially to the Earth's surface.
Sudden endogenic movements are earthquakes and volcanoes, mostly at plate margins.
An 1822 Chile earthquake raised the coast about 1 m; an 1885 New Zealand quake up to 3 m.
Denudation (from "denude", to strip off) is the general term for weathering and erosion.
Gravity provides the directional force for all downslope geomorphic movement.
Exfoliation occurs by pressure release (unloading) or by thermal stress, which is strongest in dry climates and high elevations.
Granular disintegration happens because dark minerals absorb more heat than light ones.
Frost weathering includes frost shattering, frost-wedging and freeze–thaw.
Salt weathering is typical of arid climates.
Mass wasting is downslope movement of soil and rock under gravity.
Carbonation: carbonic acid converts limestone into soluble calcium bicarbonate, forming caves (karst).
Hydration is the chemical addition of water, e.g. iron oxide becoming bulkier iron hydroxide.
Biological weathering is caused by lichens, mosses, plant roots and burrowing animals.
Weathering is the first step in soil formation.
The Chambal ravines and the Chos of Hoshiarpur are examples of gully erosion.
Sheet erosion removes a thin layer of soil; rills grow into gullies.
Wind moves sand by saltation (bounds), suspension (dust) and surface creep (coarse sand).
Coarse fragments left behind by wind form desert pavement; wind depressions reaching groundwater become oases.
Raindrop (splash) erosion is prevented by vegetation cover.
Fluvial erosion works by hydraulic action, corrosion, abrasion and attrition.
Attrition is the breaking of load particles by colliding with each other; abrasion is load scraping the bed.
Headward erosion moves a stream's source back upstream, lengthening the channel.
Braiding is a channel splitting around braid bars, in rivers with low slope or heavy load.
A deep narrow V-valley is a gorge; an extended gorge is a canyon.
The Grand Canyon of the Colorado River is 483 km long and 2.88 km deep.
River stages: youth (V-valleys, waterfalls), maturity (meanders), old age (deltas, braiding).
Majuli in the Brahmaputra (Assam) is the world's largest river island.
Kunchikal Falls (Varahi river, Karnataka; 455 m) is India's highest waterfall.
Jog (Gersoppa) Falls (253 m) is on the Sharavathi river.
Angel Falls (Venezuela, 979 m) is the world's highest waterfall.
Potholes are cylindrical holes drilled into river beds by stones swirling in eddies.
River terraces are stepped benches marking former valley floors.
A meander's outer bank is the eroding concave cliff-slope; the inner bank is the depositing convex slip-off slope.
Kanwar Lake (Begusarai, Bihar) is the largest oxbow lake in India/Asia.
A peneplain, a near-flat plain with low residual hills, is the end product of the erosion cycle.
Alluvial fans form where streams leave mountains, as along the Himalayan foothills.
Natural levees are low ridges along river banks; a breach causes sudden floods (Hwang Ho).
Deltas form as river speed falls on entering the sea and clay coagulates in salt water.
Arcuate deltas are fan-shaped — Nile and Ganga.
The Mississippi has a bird's-foot delta.
The Tiber (Italy) has a cuspate (tooth-shaped) delta.
Narmada, Tapi and Seine form estuarine deltas.
An abandoned delta forms when a river shifts its mouth — Yellow River; western Ganga delta (Hooghly).
A lacustrine delta forms where a river enters a lake.
The Narmada flows west through a linear rift valley because the land slopes west from Central India (UPSC 2013).
Glacier types are continental (ice sheets), ice caps, piedmont and valley (Alpine) glaciers.
Continental glaciers (ice sheets) are found in Antarctica and Greenland.
Piedmont glaciers form at mountain bases, as in southern Alaska.
Siachen (Karakoram, about 72 km) is India's largest glacier; Gangotri is about 25.5 km long.
A glacial trough is a U-shaped valley.
A hanging valley is a tributary glacier's valley left high above the main valley.
A horn is a peak cut by glaciers from more than two sides.
A drumlin is an inverted-boat-shaped glacial deposit.
Kettle holes are basins formed where glacial deposits sag.
Kame terraces form from sediment in ponds between glacier ice and the valley side.
Eskers are often used for making roads.
Moraines are glacial debris — ground and end (terminal), also lateral and medial.
An outwash (till) plain is the stratified deposit left where a glacier melts.
Mountains rise only about 1,500 m above their snowline; near the equator the snowline is about 5,500 m.
A bolson is an intermontane basin in a dry region.
A pediment is an erosional rock-cut surface at a mountain foot (unlike a depositional alluvial fan).
A bajada is formed by coalescing alluvial fans between pediment and playa.
Deflation basins (blowouts) are hollows scooped out by wind.
A mushroom rock is also called a pedestal rock.
An inselberg (monadnock) is an isolated hill rising abruptly from a plain.
Demoiselles are rock pillars of hard rock standing above soft rock.
Zeugen are table-shaped ridges of resistant rock over softer rock.
Wind abrasion makes wind windows that widen into wind bridges.
Ripple marks are small depositional features made by saltation.
Transverse dunes lie perpendicular to the wind; seif dunes are long linear ridges in parallel rows.
Star dunes form under winds from many directions; parabolic dunes are U-shaped with tips upwind, held by vegetation.
Thick loess occurs along the Yellow River (China) and near the Missouri River in Iowa (USA).
Deserts receive less than about 250 mm of rain a year.
Desert types: subtropical (Sahara), cold (Gobi, Atacama), coastal (Namib) and rain-shadow (Mojave, Patagonia).
The largest desert is the polar Antarctic desert (about 14.2 million km²).
Karst is named after the Karst region of former Yugoslavia on the Adriatic coast.
Pure limestone is calcium carbonate; with magnesium it is dolomite.
Karst regions have little surface drainage; water flows underground.
Surface streams disappear underground through swallow holes.
Dolines join into uvalas, and uvalas coalesce into U-shaped poljes.
A karst valley in which a stream disappears is a blind valley.
A cave with openings at both ends is a tunnel.
Stalactites hang from cave ceilings; stalagmites rise from the floor; joined they form columns.
Sinking creeks with open tops are called bogas.
Karst caves in India occur in Bastar, Dehradun and the Shillong plateau.
Borra Caves lie in the Ananthagiri hills of Andhra Pradesh.
Belum Caves (Kurnool region, AP) are the second-largest cave system in India.
A chasm is a narrow deep notch cut by waves along weak planes, widening into a bay.
A wave-cut platform is the flat bench left as a cliff retreats, with a notch at the cliff foot.
A sea cave becomes a sea arch, whose collapse leaves a stack (skerry/chimney rock).
A bar is a submerged offshore sand ridge; a barrier is its above-water counterpart; water behind is a lagoon.
A spit is a sand ridge joined to land at one end; a short curved spit is a hook.
A ria coast (drowned river valleys) is typified by south-west Ireland.
Fjord coasts are typified by Norway.
India's west coast is largely submergent and the east coast emergent.
Pulicat Lake on the AP–Tamil Nadu border is a lagoon behind Sriharikota island, second to Chilika.
Mountains typically rise above 600 m; plateaus over 300 m above their surroundings.
The Himalayas are young fold mountains; the Aravalli are old fold mountains.
Sierra Nevada (USA) and the Harz (Germany) are fault-block mountains with a steep front and gentle back.
The Andes (7,000 km) is the longest continental range; Aconcagua (6,961 m) is its highest peak.
The Lithium Triangle (Argentina, Bolivia, Chile) lies in the Andes.
Mount Elbert (4,401 m, Colorado) is the highest peak of the Rockies.
Kosciuszko (2,228 m) is the highest peak of the Great Dividing Range, source of the Murray–Darling.
The young-fold Atlas Mountains (highest Toubkal) separate the Sahara from the coast.
The old-fold Urals (highest Narodnaya) form the traditional Europe–Asia boundary.
The Appalachians are very old fold mountains (~480 million years); highest peak Mount Mitchell.
The Himalayas (Everest 8,849 m) are called the Water Tower of Asia.
The Alps are young fold mountains (~30 million years); Mont Blanc (4,809 m) is the highest.
Thabana Ntlenyana (3,482 m, Lesotho) is the highest peak of the Drakensberg.
Belukha is the highest peak of the Altai; Galdhopiggen of the Scandinavian mountains.
The Tibetan Plateau, the world's largest and highest, is an intermontane plateau called the Roof of the World.
Plateau types: intermontane, volcanic (Deccan), erosional (Colorado), dissected (Ozark) and continental (Katanga).
The Deccan, a volcanic plateau between the Western and Eastern Ghats, is India's largest plateau.
The Kimberley Plateau (Australia) has kimberlite, a diamond-bearing rock.
The Katanga Plateau (DR Congo) is known for copper and uranium.
The Laurentian Plateau is the Canadian Shield, rich in iron ore.
The Mexican Plateau ("Mineral Store") has the world's largest silver mine (Chihuahua).
The Altiplano (Peru–Bolivia) is known for tin.
The Patagonian Plateau is a rain-shadow semi-desert famous for sheep rearing.
The Anatolian Plateau (Turkey) is famous for Angora goats.
Massif Central (France) is famous for grapes.
The Loess (Huangtu) Plateau of China has the most erodible soil in the world.
The Pothohar Plateau (Pakistan) lies between the Jhelum and Indus, with the Salt Range to the south.
The Mascarene Plateau is an undersea granite remnant of Gondwana, second to the Kerguelen.
The Ahaggar (Hoggar) Plateau is a volcanic basalt plateau in the Algerian Sahara.
The Chota Nagpur Plateau is India's mineral heartland.
